note: Per-shelf attributes for the Natural Earth 1:10m ice-shelf polygons. Each number carries its source and a confidence. 'estimate' means derived or judged here, not measured. Many areas come from search snippets or secondary sources (marked medium or low). No value was invented to fill a gap: a gap is null with the dataset that would fill it. Game rules only, not navigation advice. Researched 2026-11-24 with web search only; escholarship.org (full Rignot et al. 2013 Table 1) could not be read.

confidence_scale.high: confirmed in a primary or official source this session
confidence_scale.medium: from a search snippet of a primary source, or a reliable secondary source
confidence_scale.low: secondary or popular source, or an identification by location only
confidence_scale.estimate: derived here (hydrostatics, geometry) or judged; not a measurement

front_epoch_years.source: Natural Earth ice shelves are generalised from the 2003-04 MODIS Mosaic of Antarctica, with later collapses digitised (naturalearthdata.com/?p=1488; purl.stanford.edu/my556bx0395)
front_epoch_years.note: The exact front date of each polygon is not published. Events after 2012 are treated as not shown; events before 2003 as shown; events in between as unknown unless an entry says why.

rho_ice_kgm3.source: BedMachine Antarctica, Morlighem 2020, NSIDC-0756 v2, doi:10.5067/E1QL9HFQ7A8M

rho_seawater_kgm3.source: BedMachine Antarctica, Morlighem 2020, NSIDC-0756 v2, doi:10.5067/E1QL9HFQ7A8M

freeboard_fraction.source: derived: 1 - 917/1027 = 0.107 for solid ice; firn (less dense surface snow) raises it, upper value 0.15 judged

hydrostatics.rule: freeboard = f x H; draft = (1 - f) x H, for front thickness H. A floating front always has water deeper than its draft.

thickness_m.source: spread of the sourced front thicknesses below: Filchner 150-220 m, A68 235 m, A81 (Brunt) 150 m, Abbot 200-325 m, Drygalski 300 m, Ross and Amery under 300 m

freeboard_m.source: derived from thickness_m with freeboard_fraction; matches the observed Ross cliff of 15-50 m (USGS ROSETTA-Ice; J. Glaciol.)

shelves.label: Ross Ice Shelf

area_km2_reference.source: Rignot et al. 2013, Science 341:266, Table 1: Ross West 306,105 + Ross East 194,704 km2 (search snippet)

thickness_front_m.source: USGS ROSETTA-Ice: about 1,200 m near the grounding line, under 300 m near the front

freeboard_front_m.source: 15-50 m in general; 20-40 m from Cape Crozier to King Edward VII Land (USGS ROSETTA-Ice; J. Glaciol.)

draft_front_m.basis: derived from the 20-40 m typical freeboard, capped by the 300 m front thickness

water_depth_front_m.gap: BedMachine NSIDC-0756 sea-floor depth along the front

cavity_seabed_m.source: mean sea-floor depth in the cavity: about 670 m west, 560 m east (J. Glaciol. 2025, basal reflectance and melt rates across the Ross Ice Shelf)

area_km2.source: Wikipedia Iceberg B-15; NASA gives 10,878 km2

notes: Ships have long fixed the Ross front by radar range and bearing (J. Glaciol.).
Not a front value: Wikipedia gives a freeboard under 2 m at Scott Base, which sits on the McMurdo Ice Shelf, not at the Ross calving front (confidence low; no primary source).

shelves.label: Filchner Ice Shelf

thickness_front_m.source: about 150-220 m just inland of the Filchner front, 320 m at 54 km south (radio-echo survey, Polarforschung 1981)

water_depth_front_m.gap: BedMachine NSIDC-0756 sea-floor depth along the front

notes: Filchner-Ronne fronts are low in places, about 10-20 m (search summary; the 1979-80 front-height survey was not read). Confidence low.
A23a grounded about 73 km off South Georgia in March 2025, drifted again by July 2025 and was breaking up from September 2025 (Wikipedia). It is an iceberg now; see ICEBERGS.md.

shelves.label: Ronne Ice Shelf

freeboard_front_m.gap: no sourced value; fronts low in places, about 10-20 m (search summary, low)

water_depth_front_m.gap: BedMachine NSIDC-0756 sea-floor depth along the front

notes: The Ronne front also advanced: about +5,889 km2 from 2009 to 2019 (Andreasen, Hogg and Selley 2023, doi:10.5194/tc-17-2059-2023). So the Natural Earth front can be behind the real one in places and ahead of it in others.

area_km2_reference.note: The Natural Earth polygon is about 79,600 km2 (computed) and contains 75.5 S 26 W (Brunt) and 74.9 S 22.5 W (Stancomb-Wills), so it holds those shelves too (estimate by location).

Brunt front from A81 thickness: freeboard about 15-25 m, draft about 125-135 m (estimate, hydrostatics block).

freeboard_m.basis: derived from thickness_m (a mean, so the front is likely thinner)

point_features.name: 79N Glacier (Nioghalvfjerdsbrae) floating tongue
point_features.location_note: approximate; not an outline. Two fronts: north to Dijmphna Sund and east, pinned on ice rises

freeboard_m.basis: derived from thickness_m: 80 x 0.107 = 8.6 m, 100 x 0.15 = 15 m, rounded outwards

surface.rule: A surface ship never enters an ice shelf. The front is a cliff; there is no way in.

front_caution_nm.source: no authoritative figure found; about 1-2 nm from active fronts because of calving and capsizing bergs, upper value used

surface.small_ice: Growlers (under 1 m high) and bergy bits (1-5 m high) gather near fronts (Bowditch, American Practical Navigator, ch. 32).

submarine.rule: A submarine never enters the cavity under a shelf and keeps a stand-off from the front.

standoff_nm.source: no authoritative figure found; upper end of the 1-2 nm front stand-off estimate

why: The front draft is about 125-295 m (generic estimate above), so the ice face reaches normal submarine depths.
The water column in the cavity tapers to zero at the grounding line (BedMachine Antarctica, NSIDC-0756).
Under the shelf there is no GNSS, no radio and no way to surface. The ice base is rough.
Even research robots are lost there: the Ran AUV went over 1,000 km under ice, reached 17 km into a cavity, and was lost under the ice in 2024 (University of East Anglia via EurekAlert).
Calved bergs near the front have drafts of the same order (see ICEBERGS.md).

charting.s57: Object ICEARE (code 66), attribute CATICE. Values: 1 fast ice, 2 sea ice, 3 growler area, 4 pancake ice, 5 glacier, 6 ice peak, 7 pack ice, 8 polar ice. There is no ice-shelf value, so a shelf charts as glacier (5) with the ice-front line (IHO S-57 Ed 3.1).
charting.s4: IHO S-4 B-353.8: black ice-front symbol INT1 N60.1 where a glacier meets the sea, dated if useful (IHO CSPCWG letter 07-2014).
charting.sailing_directions: NGA Pub. 200 Sailing Directions (Antarctica), 12th edition 2020; contents not read.

cliff_return.source: ice cliffs of 20-50 m give strong returns; the face toward the radar is bright in SAR (ESA); ships fix the Ross front by radar (J. Glaciol.)

horizon_rule.value: radar horizon over a smooth sea with a 4/3 effective Earth radius, antenna height plus cliff freeboard
horizon_rule.example: 25 m antenna and 30 m cliff: about 23 nm (estimate)

small_ice.value: growlers ~0.5 nm or not at all on conventional radar; lost in sea clutter in heavy seas
small_ice.source: Canadian Coast Guard ice hazard radar paper; Radar and ARPA Manual (growler echoes comparable to sea clutter)

c_ice_ms.source: typical compressional sound speed in glacier ice (research summary)

face_reflection.value: about 0.4 (about -8 dB) at normal incidence, from the impedance contrast
face_reflection.note: A rough ice face and base scatter much of this. Treat it as a strong reflector, not a mirror.

calving_noise_db.source: DOSITS 2022 (Bowdoin Glacier); JASA 2022 Greenland calving study; Dziak et al. 2013, Oceanography 26(2) (A53a); NOAA PMEL

ambient.value: ice cracking and bubble release raise broadband noise near fronts; levels of 120-140 dB re 1 uPa2/Hz below 200 Hz near glacier fronts
ambient.source: JASA 2022 Greenland calving study; Glowacki 2020, The Cryosphere 14:1025

katabatic.value: over 20-35 m/s in Terra Nova Bay and Ross Ice Shelf polynya events, air below -25 C; off the Nansen edge 35 m/s falls to 18 m/s over 99 km
katabatic.source: NSF PAR 10372596 (inside katabatic winds over the Terra Nova Bay polynya); Clim. Dyn. 2023

heat_flux.value: sensible heat flux up to 2,000 W/m2 over the polynya

fog.value: sea smoke is likely over polynyas in katabatic outbreaks; no fog climatology found
fog.source: inferred from the heat flux; no direct source
